abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev’s downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.

sections.body: Dialogue and collaborative agents repeatedly infer what a partner knows, believes, or intends. The section proposes TypeSafe Jev, a typed decision model that returns a selection and candidate probabilities as structured output, as a component for these bounded judgments. It asks how competitive and reliable Jev is as a bounded ToM decision component. The Jev-ToM framework compares five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 questions from nine existing ToM benchmarks, grouped into six capability groups. It also examines confidence-based selection, supplied reasons, output validity, observed time, and reference cost.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Assistants need repeated mental-state judgments, so this paper asks whether typed model Jev is a competitive selection component.

sections.body: The section reviews work that uses mental-state judgments in cooperative planning, dialogue, response selection, and action prediction. It notes that ToM benchmarks differ in what successful judgment requires, so scope and aggregation choices shape any ToM score. It describes Jev as a typed interface and notes that Mnemon uses Jev to evaluate retrieved records while an LLM plans searches and composes responses. Prior Jev evaluations cover task performance, calibration, and resource use, along with adversarial and option-definition sensitivity. The section states that this paper extends them to cross-benchmark ToM profiles, confidence-based selection, bidirectional changes under supplied reasons, and output validity.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier Jev studies cover accuracy, calibration, and adversarial sensitivity, but not cross-benchmark ToM profiles with supplied reasons.

sections.body: Questions are grouped by the mental states they concern: knowledge access, beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, emotions, social pragmatics, and mental-state application. Nine existing benchmarks with English contexts, reference answers, and discrete candidates are converted into a shared record with source and family identifiers. Candidate counts range from two to fifteen. The section excludes 50 BigToM items whose stories omit the event the reference requires, leaving 11,117 frozen questions. Strict scoring counts invalid or unparsed outputs as wrong, and overall accuracy weights benchmarks equally. The capability mapping review was agent-assisted and was not independent human validation.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Questions are grouped into six capability groups from nine benchmarks, with unequal source coverage across groups.

sections.body: The section compares typed and generative models on accuracy, confidence, supplied reasons, feedback, and cost. Jev reaches 73.2% overall and ranks first or second in every capability, with emotions at 84.8%. Removing native controls reverses its lead over one generative baseline, 69.1% against 70.9%. At a 0.90 confidence cutoff, retained error is 34.9% on SimpleToM, so coverage alone does not indicate reliability. Aligned supplied reasons repair some answers, but their gains shrink on new materials. Question cues account for 10.75 of Jev's 14.5-point gain on the feedback set. The section states that the 0.90 cutoff is descriptive and not a validated policy.
sections.heading: Results and Analysis
sections.headline: Jev ranks first or second in all six capabilities, but benchmark rankings reverse when native controls are removed.

sections.body: The conclusion states that Jev combines competitive bounded ToM selection with favorable reference-cost and observed-time comparisons in the evaluated deployments. It attributes benchmark-dependent confidence errors and sensitivity to supplied reasons to the insufficiency of accuracy alone for adoption. The section recommends prioritizing task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation before testing Jev within complete assistants.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Jev combines competitive bounded selection with favorable cost and time, but accuracy alone is insufficient for adoption.

sections.body: The section states that evaluation is limited to English, text-based questions with supplied candidates, so results do not establish generalization to other languages, cultures, or multimodal situations. The six capability groups are not an exhaustive measure of ToM. Possible training exposure to the public benchmarks cannot be excluded. Jev is evaluated as a component without a complete interactive assistant, so candidate generation, partner-state updates, and task success are outside the empirical claims. The confidence and reason analyses are exploratory, and the 0.90 cutoff is not a validated acceptance policy.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Results cover only English text questions with supplied candidates, and the 0.90 cutoff is not a validated policy.

sections.body: The study uses existing benchmark situations, model outputs, and annotations by three postgraduate students. It does not infer sensitive attributes of real users. The section warns that predictions about beliefs or intentions can harm users when treated as facts, so applications should separate observed information from inferred states. The supplied reasons are experimental candidate text generated and separately reviewed by a language model, not explanations produced by the evaluated models. The authors plan a versioned release of materials, identifiers, predictions, and scoring code, subject to the original licenses.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: The study uses existing benchmarks and annotations, and reason materials are experimental text rather than model explanations.

sections.body: The appendix contains extended related work on ToM benchmarks and Jev evaluations, the evaluation protocol and aggregation rules, and capability and benchmark breakdowns. It also gives confidence risk-coverage details, reason material construction and six-condition results, a resource table, and the prompt texts. Table 10 removes 920 native controls, reducing Jev from 73.2% to 69.1%. Primary comparisons use 5,000 bootstrap draws that resample source-defined families within each benchmark.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists related work, protocol, breakdowns, confidence and reason details, resource tables, and prompts.
